tasks.title: next_cursor(): encode a base64 keyset cursor
tasks.description: Implement `next_cursor(array $rows, string $orderBy): ?string` for keyset (cursor) pagination. $rows is an already-sorted list of associative rows and every row has the key $orderBy. Return the cursor a client sends back to request the next page: base64_encode((string) of the last row's $orderBy value), or null when $rows is empty (no next page). Example 1: next_cursor([['id' => 3, 'title' => 'A'], ['id' => 8, 'title' => 'B']], 'id') returns 'OA==' (base64 of '8'). Example 2: next_cursor([], 'id') returns null.

tasks.title: decode_cursor(): null sentinel wrongly returns []
tasks.description: decode_cursor(?string $cursor): ?array decodes the base64 JSON cursor produced by the encoder: a null or empty-string cursor means 'no further page' and MUST return null, because callers check `=== null` to decide when to stop paginating. A well-formed cursor returns the associative array it contains (e.g. ['id' => 42, 'sort' => 7]); malformed input — invalid base64 or base64 of something that is not a JSON object/array — also returns null. Hint: the bug is wrong null handling — the broken branch returns [] for the null/'' sentinel, so the strict `=== null` check never fires and clients paginate forever.

tasks.title: Keep a Laravel API alive through a 10-20x peak-traffic spike
tasks.description: A Laravel REST API for a multi-tenant B2B SaaS runs at roughly 200 requests/second on a handful of instances, but a marketing push or one large tenant's campaign can spike traffic 10-20x for minutes to hours. Walk through how you would design the application and its infrastructure so it survives the spike with graceful degradation instead of falling over. Cover stateless app servers and session storage, a cache-first caching strategy, queue backpressure, database read replicas, autoscaling, graceful-degradation behaviour, and observability — and justify each decision.
tasks.solution:
Make every app server stateless and disposable: store sessions in Redis (SESSION_DRIVER=redis), keep uploads and generated artifacts in object storage, and ensure any instance behind the load balancer can serve any request — a spike is handled by adding instances, never by keeping sticky state alive. Autoscale horizontally on CPU utilization, request latency, and queue depth, and make boot fast: config:cache, route:cache, OPcache, and a prebuilt container image in a warm target group, so new capacity is ready in seconds rather than minutes.

Go cache-first on shared Redis, never per-instance memory: hot queries, tenant/quota lookups, and expensive computed responses are served from cache with short TTLs, and the database is the fallback rather than the hot path. A shared cache also avoids the cold-cache stampede that would hit every fresh instance. Push all non-critical side effects — webhooks, emails, feed or report generation, AI calls — onto the queue so HTTP requests never block on slow work, and let the queue absorb the spike: scale workers, batch work, and delay or drop low-priority jobs instead of rejecting requests. Give retries exponential backoff plus a dead-letter policy so a saturated queue cannot trigger a retry storm.

Send reads to MySQL read replicas while writes stay master-only, accept small replica lag for non-critical queries, and fall back reads to the master when a replica lags too far. Under overload, degrade deliberately: per-tenant rate limiting, short timeouts and circuit breakers around external dependencies, and stale-cache fallbacks when a dependency or the database is slow — shed optional features first. Finally, make behaviour visible: structured logs and request tracing, plus metrics for queue depth, replica lag, cache hit ratio, p95 latency, and error rate, feeding dashboards and alerts that drive the autoscaling and degradation decisions, with a runbook rehearsed for the spike.

criteria: Statelessness: sessions and state externalized to Redis/object storage, no sticky sessions or per-instance storage assumptions
Scaling: horizontal autoscaling triggers and fast instance bootstrapping (config/route caches, OPcache, prebuilt images)
Caching: cache-first design on shared Redis with sane TTLs and a stampede-avoidance story
Queues: async processing of side effects with backpressure, worker scaling, and a safe retry/backoff policy
Database: read/write split with replicas, replica-lag awareness, and fallback when a replica falls behind
Graceful degradation: per-tenant rate limiting, timeouts, circuit breakers, stale-cache fallbacks, shedding optional features
Observability: metrics, structured logs, and tracing wired to dashboards and alerts that drive the scaling decisions
key_points: Redis-backed sessions let any stateless instance serve any request; no session files on instance disks
Stateless containers behind a load balancer, autoscaling on CPU/latency/queue depth
config:cache + route:cache + OPcache + a prebuilt image keep instance boot in seconds during a spike
Cache-first with shared Redis and short TTLs; the database is the fallback, not the hot path
Side effects go to queues with worker autoscaling, batching, and exponential backoff to avoid retry storms
Reads hit replicas, writes stay master-only; monitor replication lag and route reads to the master when lag is high
Per-tenant rate limiting and circuit breakers on external calls; serve stale cache during dependency outages
Track queue depth, replica lag, cache hit ratio, p95 latency, and error rate in dashboards with alerts and runbooks

tasks.title: rate_limit_ok: fixed-window rate-limit check
tasks.description: Implement rate_limit_ok(array $timestamps, int $limit, int $windowSeconds, int $now): bool. It is a fixed-window rate limiter: $timestamps holds the seconds (int) of previous requests. It returns true when a request at $now would still be within the limit — i.e. the number of previous timestamps that fall strictly inside the window (t > $now - $windowSeconds) is fewer than $limit. Examples: rate_limit_ok([], 2, 60, 100) returns true; rate_limit_ok([50, 55], 2, 60, 100) returns false (2 requests in the last 60s); rate_limit_ok([10, 55], 2, 60, 100) returns true (the request at 10 has expired); rate_limit_ok([40], 1, 60, 100) returns true (the request at exactly the window edge has expired).

tasks.title: rate_limit_ok counts the window edge as in-window
tasks.description: rate_limit_ok(array $timestamps, int $limit, int $windowSeconds, int $now): bool must count only timestamps strictly AFTER the window start ($now - $windowSeconds). A timestamp exactly at the window edge has already expired and must NOT be counted. The broken version uses >= instead of >, so the edge request is still counted and a client is wrongly throttled. Fix the boundary comparison.
